input: The analogy between the transfer processes may be stated, in the form employed by the Chilton-Colburn analogy, as follows: provided the resistance at a surface is of the same character for momentum transfer as it is for mass transfer, the behaviour of the one process is tied to the behaviour of the other, the relationship being expressed by $j_D$ = $f$/2 under those conditions in which the friction is generated within the same surface layer in which the transfer itself takes place. A brief numerical check shows the content of the statement. Taking $f$ = 0.0064, the analogy yields $j_D$ = 0.0032, exactly one half of the friction value; any measured transfer rate departing from this figure departs from the analogy rather than from the arithmetic. The analogy is, however, subject to an important qualification, which follows from the origin of the friction. Skin friction is generated in the layer immediately adjacent to the surface, and since transfer across that layer is governed by the same layer, the connection between the two factors rests on a physical basis. By contrast, where the drag takes the form of form drag, as in flow across a tube bank, the measured friction incorporates a pressure force acting on the body as a whole, for which there is no counterpart in the transfer process, and the analogy no longer holds.
target: The analogy between the transfer processes is the working assumption behind the Chilton-Colburn analogy: where the resistance at a surface is of one kind for momentum and for mass, the two transfer behaviours are tied together, and the analogy states the tie as $j_D$ = $f$/2 under the conditions in which the friction is generated in the same surface layer as the transfer. A short check shows what the statement amounts to in numbers. For $f$ = 0.0064, the analogy gives $j_D$ = 0.0032, exactly half the friction value, and a measured transfer rate that departs from the figure departs from the analogy rather than from the arithmetic. The qualification follows from where the friction comes from. Skin friction is generated in the layer at the surface, and transfer across that layer is governed by the same layer, so the tie between the factors has a physical basis. Where the drag on the surface is form drag, as in flow across a tube bank, the measured friction collects a pressure force exerted on the body as a whole. That force has no counterpart in the transfer process, the two factors separate, and the analogy fails.
